clue.text: Outlaw's advice to footpad to conceal identity

parts.note: a footpad is a highway robber on foot, so the advice to one is simply to steal: rob
wearing a hood keeps one's face hidden: in hood

explanation.surface: A famous bandit gives a fellow robber tips on staying anonymous.
explanation.walkthrough: The outlaw's name, split as ROB / IN HOOD, reads as the very advice described.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary bandit of Sherwood Forest is England's best-known outlaw.

clue.text: Unstable, like a girl's best friend?

explanation.surface: A wobbly woman is compared to her best friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diamonds are a girl's best friend', and a diamond is slangily a rock; so like one is rocky.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaky or wobbly; also, whimsically, resembling a rock, slang for a diamond.

clue.text: American town went ahead and copied Sikes

parts.note: burg is American slang for a town
led means went in front

explanation.surface: An American town rushed to imitate a notorious figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Sikes is the housebreaker in Dickens's Oliver Twist; to copy him is to break into houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill Sikes was a housebreaker, so imitating him means having broken in to steal.

clue.text: Like Ben Jonson's " jovial drink

parts.note: Jonson's song Drink to Me Only mentions Jove's nectar; 'jovial' is read as belonging to Jove, king of the gods

explanation.surface: Describing the merry drink in a poem by Ben Jonson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jovial' is read as 'of Jove': the line is 'But might I of Jove's nectar sup'.
explanation.definitionFit: Of or like nectar, the drink of the gods, which Jonson calls Jove's.

clue.text: White film star's original setting?

parts.note: Pearl White was a silent film star; a pearl's original setting is the mollusc's casing in which it grows

explanation.surface: Asks where a pale-faced actor was first placed in a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearl White starred in silent serials such as The Perils of Pauline; a pearl first grows inside a bivalve's casing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pearl forms inside a bivalve before it is ever set in jewellery.

clue.text: Performed sometimes as an auxiliary

explanation.surface: Someone performed, occasionally as a backing player.
explanation.walkthrough: As an auxiliary verb, as in 'I did go', it supports another verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of carry out; also a helping verb used for emphasis or questions.

clue.text: Office workers put notes on this

explanation.surface: Clerks scribble their memos on something.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the musical stave, the five lines on which notes are written.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm's employees are its personnel; in music the five-line stave carries the written notes.

clue.text: Scornfully reject the daily do-gooder

explanation.surface: Someone scorns the person who does good every day.
explanation.walkthrough: Boy Scouts are taught to do a good deed every day.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss an idea with contempt; also a member of the youth movement pledged to a daily good turn.

clue.text: Assuage hunger with a soft sort of pudding

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for soft
pease pudding is a dish of boiled split peas

explanation.surface: Someone satisfies their appetite with a mushy pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Pease pudding is a traditional northern English dish of boiled split peas.
explanation.definitionFit: To pacify or satisfy an appetite is to placate it.

clue.text: Belligerent fellow insists on hot dinners

explanation.surface: An aggressive man demands his meals be served hot.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: a fairground performer who swallows flames.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot-tempered, quarrelsome person; literally, a circus act who swallows flames.

clue.text: Road transport bill, as calling for capital

parts.note: a car is a vehicle for travel by road
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: Someone tots up a motoring bill needed for an outlay of capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Caracas is the capital city of Venezuela.

clue.text: Dispenser of liquid to Twickenham goal-scorer?

explanation.surface: A pipette is handed over to a rugby kicker.
explanation.walkthrough: Twickenham is England's national rugby ground; a drop goal is kicked from a ball dropped to the ground, so the pun names its scorer by the kick.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipette releasing liquid drop by drop; whimsically, a rugby player scoring with a drop kick.

clue.text: Crimean War conference venue

parts.note: looks like a meeting about the 1850s Crimean War, but means the place in Crimea of a wartime summit of 1945

explanation.surface: Where diplomats met to discuss the Crimean War.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Crimean War' not as the 1850s conflict but as a Crimean meeting during the Second World War, where Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1945 Allied summit of Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin took place at this Black Sea resort.

clue.text: Former head came round at one to discourse

parts.note: ex- as a prefix means former

indicators.note: the head comes round, enclosing the following words

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An old headmaster turned up at one o'clock to give a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'came round' signals the head enclosing the next two pieces; pate is an old word, so 'head' is easy to read as a headmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: To expatiate is to speak or write at length on a subject, to hold forth.

clue.text: Chap is a liar anyhow, full of hypocrisy

indicators.note: anyhow means in any old fashion, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A man is a liar anyway, thoroughly two-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pharisees are portrayed in the Gospels as self-righteous, so their name became a byword for sanctimony.

clue.text: Go in search of pleasure or a tribe

explanation.surface: Someone goes out on the town, or joins a tribe.
explanation.walkthrough: Gad was one of the twelve tribes of Israel; to gad about is to roam seeking fun.
explanation.definitionFit: To gad about is to wander pleasure-seeking; Gad is also one of the twelve Israelite tribes.

clue.text: One happy to air differences in the arena

definitions.text: One happy to air differences in the arena

parts.note: glad means happy

indicators.note: differences suggests the letters are rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys arguing in public debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'differences' rearranges TO AIR into IATOR; the whole clue also describes a Roman arena fighter.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman combatant fought in the amphitheatre, settling disputes by combat.

clue.text: Enthralling and stirring 'Le Mans event'

indicators.note: stirring mixes these letters up into a new order

explanation.surface: The famous 24-hour motor race at Le Mans is gripping and exciting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enthralling' looks like an adjective but is the noun: the act of making someone a thrall, a slave.
explanation.definitionFit: To enthral originally meant to make a thrall, a bondsman, of someone, so enthralling is subjugation.

clue.text: Furies evoked from you many d—'s, you say?

indicators.note: you say signals that the clue words are spoken and heard alike

parts.note: spoken, 'you many dees' runs together as the Greek name

explanation.surface: The avenging spirits are called up by repeated curses.
explanation.walkthrough: The Furies of Greek myth were euphemistically called the Kindly Ones; 'you many d's' read out sounds like their Greek name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Erinyes, Greek avenging goddesses, were placatingly called by this name, meaning Kindly Ones.

clue.text: Sent in a worker, remedying MI's industrial trouble

indicators.note: the word sent goes inside the following pieces

parts.note: a worker is a kind of bee

indicators.note: remedying puts the letters right, rearranging them

explanation.surface: Management sends in a worker to fix a security service's labour problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' and 'remedying' are the indicators; MI is Britain's military intelligence, so 'MI's' looks like the security service.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitual staying away from work is a classic industrial problem for employers.

clue.text: Valerian placed like Humpty Dumpty

parts.note: set means placed
Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall in the nursery rhyme

explanation.surface: A herb is set like the nursery rhyme's egg.
explanation.definitionFit: This old name belongs to the garden heliotrope, a valerian plant.

clue.text: A rabbit was much attached to this baby

definitions.text: A rabbit was much attached to this baby

parts.words: A rabbit was much attached to this baby
parts.note: looks like a pet's affection, but refers to the sticky doll in the Uncle Remus tales to which Brer Rabbit became literally stuck

explanation.surface: A pet rabbit dotes on an infant.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Uncle Remus stories, Brer Fox traps Brer Rabbit with a doll made of a sticky black substance that he gets stuck to.
explanation.definitionFit: The doll in the Brer Rabbit story is made of this sticky black pitch.

clue.text: " When I lie — in her hair " (Lovelace)

definitions.text: " When I lie — in her hair " (Lovelace)

parts.words: " When I lie — in her hair " (Lovelace)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Lovelace's poem To Althea, from Prison

explanation.surface: A line of Cavalier love poetry with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Lovelace's To Althea, from Prison: the missing word describes being caught up in her hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet lies caught and knotted in the beloved's hair.

clue.text: Where Albania Introduced prohibition?

parts.note: asks where a ban sits inside the word Albania: between AL and IA, Latin for between those letters

explanation.surface: A question about when a Balkan state brought in prohibition.
explanation.walkthrough: The word Albania holds BAN, a prohibition, between AL and IA; Latin 'inter' means between, so the ban is 'inter ALIA'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means among other things, read here literally as between the letters ALIA.

clue.text: Birds are trumps

explanation.surface: Some birds are winning cards.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games to ruff is to play a trump on another suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruffs are wading birds with frilled collars; in bridge one ruffs by playing a trump card.

clue.text: A fool entering the Empire State Tavern

indicators.note: the tavern goes into the state's abbreviation

parts.note: the Empire State is New York, abbreviated NY
a tavern is an inn

explanation.surface: An idiot walks into a New York bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The Empire State is New York's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: A simpleton or silly person is a nincompoop.

clue.text: Poet is as yet 19 dn

indicators.note: 19 down is a word meaning knotted or jumbled, so these letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A writer of verse is still in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 down's answer, meaning knotted, is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: W. B. Yeats was the Irish poet of The Second Coming.

clue.text: Trade vehicles on the road

explanation.surface: Business deals involving cars on the highway.
explanation.definitionFit: To deal in goods (often illicitly) is to trade; also the flow of cars and lorries on a road.

clue.text: A police constable's new-style headgear

indicators.note: a new style rearranges these letters

explanation.surface: A policeman gets a new kind of helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: A cap is a soft peaked hat, an item of headwear.

clue.text: French boy's mark I called odd

indicators.note: odd suggests the letters are in a strange order

explanation.surface: A French lad's school grade is called strange.
explanation.walkthrough: The mark is the hook under the c in garçon, the French for boy.
explanation.definitionFit: The hook under a c in French, as in garçon, softens it to an s sound.

clue.text: Masses of eggs, about 50, in these parts

indicators.note: the eggs go around the number, enclosing it

parts.note: roes are masses of fish eggs
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Fish spawn of about fifty in these parts of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors' parts in a play are their characters.

clue.text: Fencing by assistants at the royal residence, do we hear?

indicators.note: asks whether the phrase is spoken alike, signalling a sound-alike

parts.note: helpers at a palace are palace aides

explanation.surface: Royal staff are seen sword-fighting at the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, 'palace aides' sounds like the word for rows of stakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A palisade is a fence of pointed wooden stakes, so fencing in the sense of an enclosure.
